title: Retrieval: keyword, vector, hybrid
story:
Dense retrieval represents a passage as a point in a space arranged so that things meaning similar things sit near each other, and answers a query by finding the nearest points. It handles the thing keyword matching never could: a question phrased in words the document does not contain.

Then it meets an identifier — a part number, a statute reference, an error code — and returns documents about roughly the right subject that do not contain it.

The failure is worth understanding rather than working around, because it is not a defect. An identifier has no meaning to match. Its entire value is that it is exactly itself and nothing else, and a representation built to place similar meanings near each other has nothing to work with: the string is arbitrary, its neighbours in the space are things that look or sound similar, and looking similar is precisely the wrong relation for a code where one character's difference is a different object.

So the failure is structural. It is not a weaker model or a worse index; a system built to generalise across surface forms cannot be relied on for a query whose whole content is a surface form.

The complementary tool is the older one. The standard sparse ranking function was developed from the probabilistic relevance framework by Robertson, Spärck Jones and colleagues. It scores a document by the query terms it contains, weighting rarer terms more heavily, applying saturation so that repeated occurrences give diminishing returns, and normalising for document length so long documents are not favoured merely for containing more words.

Each of those three is worth noticing, because together they are why it is still competitive. Rare terms weigh more, which is exactly what an identifier is. Saturation means a document repeating a word fifty times does not beat one using it twice in the right context. Length normalisation stops a long document winning by sheer surface area. It is not a keyword search with extra steps; it is a ranking function with the right instincts about which words matter.

And its weakness is the mirror image: a query using different words from the document finds nothing, because it matches strings and a synonym is a different string.

So run both. The interesting problem is what to do with two ranked lists, and it is harder than it looks — the two systems produce scores on entirely incomparable scales, one a similarity in a geometric space and the other an accumulation of term weights. Adding them, averaging them or weighting them requires a correspondence that does not exist, and any normalisation invents one.

The published answer avoids the problem rather than solving it. Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher presented Reciprocal Rank Fusion at SIGIR in 2009, reporting that this simple method of combining ranked result lists outperformed Condorcet fusion and individual rank learning methods. Each document is scored by summing, across the lists it appears in, one divided by a constant plus that document's rank in that list.

Only positions are used. The scores are never compared, so the incomparability stops mattering — and the reciprocal shape means the difference between first and second place counts for much more than the difference between fortieth and forty-first, which is the right behaviour when what you want is the top few. A document ranked respectably by both systems can beat one ranked first by one and ignored by the other, which is usually what you want, and occasionally is not.

Two things worth knowing. The constant is a tuning parameter that controls how much weight low ranks retain, so it is not free of choices, merely free of the worst one. And the method is indifferent to how good either list is — fusing a strong ranking with a weak one produces something between them, so it improves coverage rather than quality, and two retrievers that fail on the same query still fail together.

problem.name: Two retrievers, incomparable scores
problem.shape: A query may be about meaning or may be an exact string, and one retriever cannot serve both.
tell: exact identifiers return topically related but wrong documents
two result lists are being merged by adding or normalising their scores
evaluation queries are all phrased the way documents are
problem.move: Run a term-matching and a meaning-matching retriever together, then combine by position rather than by score, since the two scales have no correspondence. Score each document by summing the reciprocal of a constant plus its rank in each list it appears in.
problem.invariant: An identifier has no meaning to match, so a representation built to place similar meanings together cannot retrieve it. A representation built to match strings cannot retrieve a paraphrase. The two fail exactly where the other is strong.
problem.breaks: Fusion by rank improves coverage rather than quality. It is indifferent to how good either list is, so combining a strong ranking with a weak one produces something between them — and two retrievers that both fail on a query still fail together, which no fusion method repairs.

cost.time: two retrievals per query instead of one, and a fusion step
cost.space: two indexes over the same corpus, maintained and updated together
cost.beats: dense retrieval alone, which handles paraphrase and cannot find identifiers, and sparse alone, which finds identifiers and misses anything phrased differently

problem.practice: Take your retrieval evaluation set and count how many queries contain an exact identifier, and how many are phrased in words absent from the target document. If either count is zero, the suite cannot detect the corresponding failure.

beats.broke: A retriever matching meaning cannot find an identifier, because an identifier has no meaning to match — its entire value is being exactly itself, which is the one relation a semantic space does not encode.
beats.fix: Run a term-matching retriever alongside the meaning-matching one, since each fails exactly where the other is strong, and combine their rankings by position.
beats.cost: The two produce scores on incomparable scales, so they cannot be added or normalised without inventing a correspondence — the combination has to use ranks and nothing else.

interview.answer:
Because an identifier has no meaning to match, and matching meaning is the entire mechanism.

Dense retrieval places passages in a space where similar meanings sit near each other and answers a query by nearest points. An identifier's value is that it is exactly itself: the string is arbitrary, its neighbours in that space are things that look or sound similar, and looking similar is precisely the wrong relation for a code where one character's difference is a different object. So the failure is structural — a system built to generalise across surface forms cannot be relied on when the query's whole content is a surface form, and improving the embedding does not address it.

The complement is the sparse ranking function from the probabilistic relevance framework, which scores documents by query terms, weighting rarer terms more heavily, saturating so repeats give diminishing returns, and normalising for length. All three matter: rare terms weighing more is exactly what an identifier is, saturation stops a document repeating a word fifty times beating one using it twice in context, and normalisation stops a long document winning on surface area. Its weakness is the mirror image — a synonym is a different string.

So run both, and the real problem appears: the scores are on incomparable scales, one a geometric similarity and one an accumulation of term weights. Adding or normalising requires a correspondence that does not exist.

The published answer avoids it. Reciprocal Rank Fusion, presented at SIGIR in 2009 and reported to outperform Condorcet fusion and individual rank learning methods, scores each document by summing one over a constant plus its rank in each list it appears in. Only positions are used, so the scores are never compared. The reciprocal shape also makes the gap between first and second count for far more than fortieth to forty-first, which is right when you want the top few — so a document ranked respectably by both beats one ranked first by one and ignored by the other.

Two limitations: the constant is a tuning parameter controlling how much weight low ranks keep, so this is free of the worst choice rather than free of choices; and fusion is indifferent to list quality, so it improves coverage rather than quality and two retrievers that both fail still fail together.

Underneath it all is an evaluation failure: if every test query is phrased the way the documents are, neither weakness ever appears, and the system looks excellent until somebody types a part number.
